questions.question_text:
A fair coin is flipped $200$ times.
How many times would you expect it to land on heads?

options.why: This is a quarter of the trials; heads is expected on half of the $200$ flips.
This is the number of trials; it still needs to be multiplied by $P(\text{heads}) = \frac{1}{2}$.
Divided by the probability instead of multiplying: $200 \times \frac{1}{2}$ halves the trials.

questions.question_text:
A fair six-sided die is rolled $60$ times.
How many times would you expect it to land on a $3$?

options.why: Used a probability of $\frac{1}{2}$ as if flipping a coin, but a die has $6$ equally likely faces.
Divided the $60$ rolls by $5$, but a die has $6$ faces, so $P(3) = \frac{1}{6}$.
This is the number of favourable faces, not the number of trials multiplied by the probability.
Used $\frac{1}{5}$ for a single blue sector, but $2$ of the $5$ sectors are blue.
Used a probability of $\frac{1}{2}$, but blue covers $2$ of the $5$ equal sectors.
This is the number of blue sectors, not the number of trials multiplied by the probability.

questions.solution_text:
The $5$ sectors are equal and $2$ are blue.
$P(B) = \frac{2}{5}$
$f = np$
$= 40 \times \frac{2}{5}$
$= 16$

questions.question_text:
A fair ten-sided die has its faces numbered from $1$ to $10$.
It is rolled $80$ times.
What is the expected frequency of rolling an even number?

options.why: Used $\frac{1}{10}$ for a single face, but $5$ of the $10$ faces are even.
Used a probability of $\frac{2}{10}$, but the even faces are $2, 4, 6, 8, 10$ — five faces.
This is the number of even faces, not the number of trials multiplied by the probability.

questions.question_text:
The probability that a biased coin lands on heads is $\frac{2}{3}$.
The coin is flipped $90$ times.
What is the expected frequency of heads?

options.why: Used a probability of $\frac{1}{2}$ as if the coin were fair, but this coin is biased with $P(\text{heads}) = \frac{2}{3}$.
Used a probability of $\frac{1}{3}$ instead of the stated $P(\text{heads}) = \frac{2}{3}$.
Divided the trials by $\frac{2}{3}$ instead of multiplying by it.
Used $\frac{1}{10}$ for a single blue sector, but $4$ of the $10$ sectors are blue.
Used a probability of $\frac{1}{2}$, but blue covers $4$ of the $10$ equal sectors.
This is the number of blue sectors, not the number of trials multiplied by the probability.

questions.solution_text:
The $10$ sectors are equal and $4$ are blue.
$P(B) = \frac{4}{10}$
$= \frac{2}{5}$
$f = np$
$= 30 \times \frac{2}{5}$
$= 12$

questions.question_text:
A fair ten-sided die has its faces numbered from $1$ to $10$.
It is rolled $200$ times.
What is the expected frequency of rolling an $11$?

options.why: Used $\frac{1}{10}$ as if $11$ were one of the faces, but no face shows $11$.
An impossible event has probability $0$, so it is not expected to occur even once.
Used a probability of $\frac{1}{2}$, but rolling an $11$ is impossible on this die.

questions.solution_text:
No face shows $11$, so rolling an $11$ is impossible.
$P(11) = 0$
$f = np$
$= 200 \times 0$
$= 0$

questions.question_text:
A spinner has $5$ equal sectors and exactly $1$ of them is green.
How many times must the spinner be spun so that the expected frequency of green is $9$?

options.why: Added the $5$ sectors to $9$ instead of solving $9 = n \times \frac{1}{5}$.
Doubled the expected frequency, but green is expected on one fifth of the spins, so $n = 9 \times 5$.
This is the number of sectors; the number of trials comes from dividing $9$ by the probability $\frac{1}{5}$.

questions.question_text:
A spinner has $8$ equal sectors and exactly $1$ of them is yellow.
It is spun $50$ times.
What is the expected frequency of yellow?
Give the exact value as a decimal.

options.why: Rounded up to a whole number, but the question asks for the exact expected frequency, which can be a decimal.
Rounded down to a whole number, but the question asks for the exact expected frequency, which can be a decimal.
This is the number of sectors, not the expected frequency; compute $f = np = 50 \times \frac{1}{8}$.

questions.solution_text:
$P(\text{yellow}) = \frac{1}{8}$
$f = np$
$= 50 \times \frac{1}{8}$
$= 6.25$
The actual count of yellows is always a whole number, but the expected frequency can be a decimal.

questions.question_text:
The probability you win a game is $0.4$.
Assuming independent outcomes, if you played the game 200 times, how many times would you expect to lose?

options.why: Calculates the expected number of wins rather than losses.
Doubles the correct expected number of losses.
Uses the win probability as though it were a count of losses.

questions.solution_text: The probability of losing is $1-0.4=0.6$. The expected number of losses is $200\times0.6=120$.
